newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada awaits key U.S. decision on landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: Canada awaits key U.S. decision on landmine ban.

text.p: Canada is anxiously awaiting a decision on whether U.S. President (Bill) Clinton will throw his weight behind its initiative for a worldwide ban on the scourge of anti-personnel landmines.
"It would be a very, very good thing if they would come around," John English, a special representative for Canada on landmines, told Reuters.

Clinton is widely expected to decide within days whether he will give his backing to the so-called Ottawa Process, Canada's attempt to push through a treaty banning the use, transfer, stockpiling and production of landmines.

While Britain's Princess Diana leads hordes of paparazzi to devastated corners of the world in a high-profile campaign against landmines, Canada has worked quietly but aggressively to bring the world's political leaders on side.
Canada's Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, fed up with waiting for a consensus decision by the Conference on Disarmament to move forward on the issue, proposed the ban last October.
The Canadian foreign minister's Ottawa Process would make it illegal for the treaty's signatories to deal with landmines.
Up to 100 countries already have expressed support for the process and plan to show up in Oslo in two weeks to hammer out a draft text in time for a final meeting in Ottawa in December.
After much lobbying from supporters of the ban, Australia said on Friday it would sign on to the Canadian initiative. Argentina and Chile also agreed this week to give the ban their support.
But so far the process lacks the backing of some key players like major landmine producers Russia, China, India and Pakistan -- and the world's military leader, the United States.

"My impression of public opinion and newspaper editorials in the United States are overwhelmingly in favor of a landmine ban," said military analyst Alex Morrison, president of the Pearson Peacekeeping Center in Canada.
"I'm not sure why the U.S. government is being so difficult and so recalcitrant. I'm not sure they'll be able to withstand the universal international pressure on this subject."
Until now, Washington has shunned the Ottawa Process in favor of working through the Conference on Disarmament. It has objected to signing an agreement that did not include Russia and China.
The United States also faces pressure from the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who argue they should be able to use so-called "smart mines" that will self-destruct. Critics say those mines are unreliable.
Some observers have suggested Washington is loathe to agree to a treaty led and dominated by small and medium-sized powers.

From 1985 to 1996, the United States produced more than 10 million new anti-personnel mines, adding them to a stockpile of up to 18 million mines, according to Vietnam Veterans of America Foundation. The United States has a moratorium on transfer of the mines however.

Anti-personnel landmines take another victim every 22 minutes or about 26,000 victims a year, according to Canadian government estimates. Most victims are women and children in former war-ravaged areas like Cambodia, Bosnia, Central America, Afghanistan, Mozambique and Angola.
Experts say Afghanistan alone has so many buried landmines it will take centuries to clear them.
